title: The Winter Lantern
premise: In 1848, on the frozen edge of a city sliding toward revolution, Ines Whitlock has spent her life passing as her late brother in her father's print shop, cutting typefaces by day and forging nothing but quiet. When a census taker named Aurel Varga notices the discrepancy between the shop's records and its workers, he holds her secret like a blade—and then, unexpectedly, asks for her help instead: his own name is on a list of dissidents to be arrested when the ice breaks. Together they must smuggle the census ledger, which proves who was erased and who will be disappeared, past three checkpoints along the river before the thaw destroys both the evidence and their window. Ines survives the last checkpoint only by surrendering her invisibility entirely—claiming her own name aloud at gunpoint—and the book ends with the ledger burned into a thousand printed copies, her father's shop shuttered, and Ines leaving on the spring barge not as anyone's son or daughter, but as herself.
about_author: M. M. Voss is the pen name of a former letterpress compositor who spent fifteen years setting type in small-town print shops before turning to fiction. They write historical novels about people history forgot to record, drawn from the marginalia of trade ledgers and census rolls.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Letters
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. A day in the Whitlock print shop: Ines cuts typefaces with hands too skilled for a 'son' who never speaks above a whisper, while her father drinks and the city outside grows restless. Emotional beat: the comfort and suffocation of routine, establishing what she stands to lose.

chapters.title: One Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The annual census taker arrives—but this year it's a new man, Aurel Varga, whose questions drift from household size to why the apprentice listed in 1844 never appears again. Ines lies well, but he leaves looking unconvinced. Beat: first crack in the wall of her invisibility.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Keeps
chapters.summary: Aurel's POV. Alone in his office, Aurel cross-references old censuses and finds three households where children vanished from the record—Ines among them. He understands she isn't a criminal but a survivor of something unnamed. Beat: reluctant curiosity hardening into dangerous knowledge.

chapters.title: The List
chapters.summary: Aurel's POV. Summoned by his superiors, Aurel is ordered to finalize arrest lists for when the river thaws—and finds his own name among the dissidents. He realizes the census he's building is a weapon pointed at him. Beat: cold fear; the hunter learns he is prey.

chapters.title: An Offer at the Door
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Aurel returns after hours, no ledger in hand, and makes an astonishing proposal: help him smuggle the master census copy out through the checkpoints, and he'll burn her page forever. She refuses—then finds soldiers measuring the shop's windows. Beat: cornered choice.

chapters.title: Hands That Remember
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines weighs flight against fight, remembering how her family learned to disappear years ago—a memory surfacing in fragments. She agrees to Aurel's plan, but on her terms: the ledger gets printed, not just moved. Beat: agency seized; the found-family thread begins.

chapters.title: Setting the Type
chapters.summary: Dual POV alternating scenes. By night, Ines and Aurel compose pages from the ledger in the shop's back room, her father drunkenly almost discovering them. Each name set in metal feels like a resurrection. Beat: intimacy through shared labor; trust built letter by letter.

chapters.title: First Checkpoint: The Bridge of Sighs
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The printed sheets, hidden inside a coffin Aurel requisitions, pass the first checkpoint—but a guard recognizes Ines's gait as a woman's. She talks her way through by performing masculinity flawlessly, and hates how good she's become at it. Beat: triumph laced with grief.

chapters.title: The Printer's Daughter
chapters.summary: Father's POV (brief interlude). Her father, sober for one evening, reveals he always knew—and that disappearing was his idea, born of a debt to men now running the arrests. He gives her the shop's second key. Beat: painful tenderness; the price of survival made explicit.

chapters.title: Second Checkpoint: The Salt Warehouse
chapters.summary: Aurel's POV. At the warehouse checkpoint, Aurel's superior demands to inspect everything personally. Aurel sacrifices his own cover, confessing to petty corruption to explain the cargo, buying passage by making himself smaller. Beat: self-erasure mirrored; he learns what Ines has lived.

chapters.title: Ice Groaning
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Waiting out a curfew in a safehouse above a tavern, Ines and Aurel speak honestly for the first time—her brother's death, his wife already arrested. The river ice cracks audibly below. Beat: found family crystallizing under pressure; deadline tightening.

chapters.title: The Missing Page
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Discovering her own page torn from the printed run, Ines realizes someone inside their circle is trading information for safety. Suspicion falls on everyone, including Aurel. Beat: paranoia; the cost of trusting anyone in a surveillance state.

chapters.title: Third Checkpoint: The Customs House
chapters.summary: Aurel's POV. The customs house checkpoint is a trap—the torn page was bait. Aurel is detained while the sheets are seized, and he watches his life's work stacked for burning. Beat: apparent defeat; lowest point approaching.

chapters.title: Ash on the Water
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Told Aurel is arrested, Ines must choose: flee alone as planned, or stay. She stays, retrieving the hidden second printing plate her father buried beneath the shop floor years ago. Beat: resolve forged; survival redefined as more than escape.

chapters.title: The Man Who Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Aurel's POV. Interrogated by his former mentor, Aurel refuses to give up Ines even under threat, discovering that a man defined by paperwork can still be unmade by principle. Beat: moral climax for Aurel; identity as choice, not record.

chapters.title: Breaking the Shop Open
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. With soldiers coming for the press, Ines and her father work through the night printing the final run on the buried plates—her father setting type beside her for the first time as an equal. Beat: reconciliation; the shop becomes what it should have been all along.

chapters.title: The Thaw Begins
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The river cracks open early. Crowds surge toward the bridges as rumors spread that the lists are public—because copies of the ledger have begun appearing nailed to doors across the city. Someone distributed them. Beat: hope igniting out of chaos.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Zero
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Carrying the last original ledger to the river landing, Ines faces the third checkpoint one final time—and the guard with the torn page. Cornered, she does the unthinkable: she answers every question truthfully, claiming her own name aloud. Beat: climax; invisibility surrendered as an act of power.

chapters.title: What the River Takes
chapters.summary: Aurel's POV. Freed in the chaos of the spreading pamphlets, Aurel reaches the landing in time to see Ines surrounded—and vouches for her with his badge, his career, his name, burning his own file on the brazier. Beat: mutual salvation; the price paid willingly.

chapters.title: After the Ice
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The city wakes transformed—arrests stalled, censors overwhelmed, names restored to the record. Ines walks through streets where strangers read her words without knowing her face, and for once anonymity feels chosen rather than imposed. Beat: exhale; the world remade in small ways.

chapters.title: The Empty Frame
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Father and daughter close the shop together, leaving the sign reading WHITLOCK & DAUGHTER, freshly painted over her objections and to her secret delight. Aurel arrives with a barge ticket and no agenda. Beat: quiet joy; found family formalized in departure rather than staying.

chapters.title: The Winter Lantern
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, epilogue voice. On the spring barge, Ines lights a paper lantern printed with the first line of the ledger and lets it go over the water. She signs her own name in the ship's manifest—full, unhidden, hers. Beat: resolution; identity claimed, survival repurposed as beginning.
